What it does
When to reach for it

Whenever you ask 'have I seen X before?' or need value → position
Yields `(index, value)` pairs in one pass
You need both the position and the item, without `range(len(...))`
Hash lookup of the complement (average O(1))
Replaces an inner loop that would scan every earlier number
You must return positions, not values

p: `nums = [2,7,11,15]`, `target = 9`. For each `x` we look for `target - x` among numbers already stored.

The lookup happens before `seen[x] = i`, so a number can never pair with itself. With `nums = [3,3]`, `target = 6`: at `i=0`, `seen` is empty, so we store `3→0`; at `i=1`, the complement `3` is found at index 0, giving `[0,1]`. If we stored first, `[3,2,4]` with target 6 would wrongly return `[0,0]`.

blocks.h: Why a dict instead of a nested loop?
p: You pay O(n) memory to turn the inner scan into a single lookup.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass, each dict operation is O(1) on average.
Space: O(n) — the dict can hold every number before the match is found.

1.takeaway: Complement lookup in a hash map: when you need a pair satisfying a sum, remember what you have seen and ask 'is my partner already there?' in O(1) instead of rescanning.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: `if len(A) > len(B): A, B = B, A`
Swaps so `A` is the shorter list
You binary-search one array; pick the shorter so the search is O(log min(m,n)) and `j` never leaves its range
Sentinels that compare below / above every number
A cut at the very edge has no real neighbour; sentinels make the comparisons still work
Conditional expression; `i` is falsy only when 0
Guard an index lookup without a separate branch
Largest of the left half's tail, smallest of the right half's head
The median is built from the two numbers touching the cut
Standard binary search on a cut position

p: `A=[1,3]`, `B=[2]`. A is longer, so they swap to `A=[2]`, `B=[1,3]`; `m=1, n=2, half=(1+2+1)//2=2`. `i` is how many items of `A` go in the left half and `j = half − i` is how many come from `B`. Odd total (3), so the answer is `max(a_left, b_left)` = 2.
No swap (equal lengths); `half = (4+1)//2 = 2`. Even total, so the median is the average of the two numbers touching the cut: `(max(a_left,b_left) + min(a_right,b_right)) / 2` = 2.5.

blocks.h: Why binary search the shorter array, and why `half = (m+n+1)//2`?
bullets: With `m ≤ n`, every `i` in `[0, m]` gives `j = half − i` in `[0, n]`, so `B[j-1]`/`B[j]` are always safe (with the sentinels). If `A` were the longer array, `j` could go negative.
The `+1` gives the left half the extra element when the total is odd, so for odd totals the median is simply the largest item in the left half: `max(a_left, b_left)`.
The cut is valid exactly when `a_left ≤ b_right` and `b_left ≤ a_right`; each array is already sorted, so those two checks are enough.
Time: O(log min(m, n)) — each iteration halves the range of `i` over the shorter array.
Space: O(1) — only a handful of variables.

p: `a_left > b_right` means we took too many from `A` (move the cut left: `hi = i-1`); otherwise `b_left > a_right` means too few (`lo = i+1`). Moving `i` automatically moves `j` the opposite way, which keeps the left half's size fixed at `half`.

4.takeaway: Binary search on the partition, not on values: find the cut that splits the merged order into equal halves, searching only the shorter array.

p: Python integers never overflow, so the reversed value is computed exactly and then compared with the 32-bit limits. In a language with fixed-width ints you would have to detect overflow before it happens (for example, compare `r` with `INT_MAX // 10` while building digit by digit). p: The sign is stripped before reversing, because `str(-123)[::-1]` would be `'321-'`, which `int` rejects. Zero is fine: `sign = 1`, `int('0') = 0`.

7.takeaway: Reverse digits via string slicing and handle the 32-bit limit with an explicit post-check; strip the sign first so the minus never lands in the wrong place.

p: `s = 'MCMXCIV'` (1994). A symbol is subtracted when the next symbol is larger.

blocks.h: Why compare with the next character, not the previous?
p: Looking ahead lets us decide the sign of the current symbol immediately: if the next one is bigger, this one is part of a subtractive pair (`IV`, `CM`). Looking back would mean adding the earlier symbol first and then correcting it by double the amount (`total += 1` for `I`, then at `V` add `5 − 2·1`). The look-ahead needs no correction.

bullets: Time: O(n) — one pass; each step is O(1).
Space: O(1) — the dictionary has a fixed 7 entries.

p: The code never validates the numeral; it only relies on the rule that a smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted. Because inputs are valid, the sign rule alone reproduces every pair (`IV`, `IX`, `XL`, `XC`, `CD`, `CM`).

13.takeaway: Look one symbol ahead to pick the sign: a lookup table plus 'subtract if smaller than next' parses Roman numerals in one pass.

With it, `[1]` and `n = 1` work: start: fast 0, slow 0 dummy → 1; advance fast 1 times: fast fast at 1, slow slow at 0; unlink: fast fast at 1 (last), slow slow at 0 slow.next = slow.next.next removes 1 → result [] (`dummy.next` is `None`).

Space: O(1) — two pointers and one dummy node.

p: `n = 2`: the recursion explores these states (each row is one call, in order). It visits 8 calls and finds ['(())', '()()'].

blocks.h: Why these two rules and not 'try everything, then check'?
p: `close < open_` is the key: a `)` is allowed only if there is an unmatched `(` to close, so the string can never go negative. `open_ < n` stops us using more than n opens. With both, every path that reaches length 2n is automatically well-formed.

bullets: Time: O(4ⁿ/√n), the n-th Catalan number of results times the O(n) to build each string.
Space: O(n) recursion depth (2n frames), not counting the output.

22.takeaway: Backtracking with validity pruning: only extend a prefix when it can still become well-formed (opens < n, closes < opens).

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Walks up to k nodes ahead, stopping early at the end
Check whether a full group exists before changing anything
Recursion: solves the rest of the list first
The result becomes the tail attached to this group
Reversed group's last node must point to the next group

p: `1→2→3→4→5`, `k = 2`. Each row is one call (depth = recursion level). Final list: 2→1→4→3→5.

head: Depth
Sublist given
Nodes found
What happens
rows: enough nodes; recurse on rest starting at 3
enough nodes; recurse on rest starting at 5

p: At the start of a group `prev` is the node that must follow it. Each iteration does three things in order using the old values: set `cur.next = prev`, move `prev` forward to `cur`, move `cur` to its old successor. After k iterations `prev` is the group's new head and the old head (`head`) is its tail pointing at the rest. The right-hand side `prev, cur, cur.next` is fully evaluated before any assignment, which is why the old `cur.next` is not lost.

If fewer than k nodes remain, the leftovers must stay in the original order. Reversing first and undoing later would be extra work and error-prone; counting first (`cnt < k: return head`) keeps the tail untouched.

bullets: Time: O(n) — every node is walked once to count and once to reverse.
Space: O(n/k) — one stack frame per group. An iterative version with a dummy head is O(1) extra space.

25.takeaway: Reverse in groups: verify k nodes exist, reverse them by re-pointing links, and attach to the recursively solved remainder.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Scans from the right for the first position that is smaller than its right neighbour
Find where the suffix stops being non-increasing
Scans from the right for the first value strictly larger than `nums[i]`
Smallest possible bump of position i; `<=` skips equal values
Slice assignment from the reversed iterator
Reverse the tail in place of the same list

p: `nums = [1,5,8,4,7,6,5,3,1]`. The tail `7,6,5,3,1` is non-increasing (already the largest arrangement of those numbers). The dip is at `4`.

bullets: The suffix after `i` is non-increasing, i.e. the largest arrangement of its elements. To get the next permutation we must grow position `i` by the smallest amount: swap with the rightmost element larger than `nums[i]`.

After the swap the suffix is still non-increasing (the swapped-in element sits where a slightly smaller one fits). The smallest arrangement of a non-increasing run is its reverse, so one reversal finishes it in O(n).
When no dip exists (`[3,2,1]`), `i` ends at −1, the swap is skipped, and `nums[0:] = reversed(...)` wraps around to the lowest order: [1, 2, 3].
Time: O(n) — two backward scans, a swap and a reversal, each at most one pass.
Space: O(1) — in place (the reversed iterator does not copy the list, although the slice read `nums[i+1:]` creates a temporary).

p: Use `>=` in the first loop and `<=` in the second so that duplicates are handled: `[1,1,5]` should go to `[1,5,1]`, and equal neighbours must not count as a dip.

31.takeaway: Next permutation: find the rightmost ascent, swap with the next-larger value from the right, then reverse the suffix to its smallest order.

p: Small case `candidates = [1,1,2]`, `target = 4` (sorted already). The duplicate rule shows up on the second line from the bottom.

head: Event
rows: go(start=1, rem=3): take 2 (i=2) → path [1, 2]  (rem 1 left, no more items)

p: Two equal values may both appear in one combination (`[1,1,2]` above takes both 1s). The ban applies only to using the same value twice *at the same recursion level*, which would build the same combination again. `i > start` allows the second `1` as a deeper step (`start` moved to 1) but skips it as an alternative first choice at the top level (`start = 0`). Using `i > 0` would wrongly kill `[1,1,2]` too.
The list is sorted, so every later value is at least as large and also fails. `break` abandons the loop; `continue` would still be correct but waste work.

bullets: Time: O(2ⁿ) in the worst case (each element is taken or skipped).
Space: O(n) recursion depth and path, not counting the output.

40.takeaway: Sort, then backtrack with a start index; skip duplicates only at the same depth (`i > start`) and break early when the sorted values exceed the remainder.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Digit array big enough for the product
The product of an m-digit and n-digit number has at most m+n digits
Counts down from the last index to 0
Process digits from least to most significant, like pen-and-paper
Converts one character to its digit
Only single digits are converted, never the whole string
Digit and carry of a two-digit value
Convert the digit list back to text
The array is longer than needed when the product has m+n−1 digits

p: `'123' × '456'`. Digit `num1[i] × num2[j]` lands at positions `i+j` (carry) and `i+j+1` (digit). State of `res` after each outer iteration:

Digit `i` of `num1` has place value 10^(m−1−i), digit `j` of `num2` has 10^(n−1−j); their product has place value 10^(m+n−2−i−j), which is slot `i+j+1` (units digit) with a carry into slot `i+j` (tens). So the final array is [0, 5, 6, 0, 8, 8] and after `lstrip('0')` it reads `56088`. Adding `res[i+j+1]` into `p` first folds in the earlier partial products and carry.

blocks.h: Why the `"0"` guard at the top?
p: Without it, `'0' × '123'` produces `[0,0,0,0]`, `lstrip('0')` returns `''`, and the answer would be an empty string instead of `'0'`.

bullets: Time: O(m·n) — every pair of digits is multiplied once.
Space: O(m + n) for the result array.

43.takeaway: Simulate grade-school multiplication in a digit array: digits i and j land at positions i+j and i+j+1, carrying as you go.

p: The `used` version is easier to get right and explain; swapping saves memory but is harder to reason about.

bullets: Time: O(n·n!) — n! permutations, each copied in O(n).
Space: O(n) for recursion, `path` and `used` (excluding the output).

Reachable positions always form a prefix `0..reach`: if you can reach index 5 you can reach everything before it. So one number captures all the DP state, giving O(n) time and O(1) space instead of O(n²).

p: `split(' ')` cuts at every single space, so the extra spaces produce empty strings, and a trailing space would make `[-1]` equal `''` (length 0, wrong). No-argument `split()` treats any run of whitespace as one separator and drops empties.
